customManagers.description: The rules_rs toolchain version in MODULE.bazel. Named and sourced exactly as the built-in rust-toolchain manager names rust-toolchain.toml, so the two group.
The digest-pinned images rules_img's `pull` fetches, written as (name, registry, repository, tag, digest) tuples that no manager parses.

packageRules.description: Pinned by `git_override` to a commit past v0.0.1, for the `//mutants:config` support the sweep needs. The `bazel_dep` version beside it selects nothing, and the Bazel Central Registry does not serve this module at all -- a registry bump here would be a no-op that reads like a real one.

`single_version_override` applies //bazel/patches/aspect-rules-lint-rust-toolchain-pattern.patch. A bump that moves the patched lines fails to apply, and a patch failure breaks module resolution before a single target is analysed -- so this gets a pull request, but lands by hand with the patch re-checked.

MODULE.bazel and rust-toolchain.toml carry one decision in two files. They drifted apart once already -- Bazel building with 1.97.0 while Cargo used 1.97.1 -- which is the exact split the one-dependency-source arrangement exists to prevent. Grouped so they can only move together.

These images are what the differential suites compare against. Moving one changes the reference implementation, so a suite can start failing on a difference nobody in this repository introduced. That is a reading to take deliberately, not a merge to wake up to.

Every `uses:` in .github/workflows/ is pinned to a commit SHA, which is what makes a workflow run the bytes it was reviewed with rather than whatever a moving tag points at today. A digest bump is still a code change to a step that holds repository secrets and, in the delivery jobs, a registry push -- so it gets a pull request that a human reads, not a merge that happens overnight.

Both carry something a version bump can break quietly. rules_rs is patched by //bazel/patches/rules-rs-target-has-atomic.patch and //bazel/patches/rules_rs_zlib_url.patch, and a patch that still applies with fuzz can land on lines that no longer mean what they did -- a build that succeeds while generating something else. llvm is a registered toolchain, so it is the C++ compiler every cc dependency in the graph is built with. Neither is a merge to wake up to.

The sibling crates reach this repository through [patch.crates-io], which Renovate's Cargo manager does not read -- it sees only the `version = "0.4.0"` in each member manifest and takes them for registry dependencies. Those versions are a formality: the patch table decides what is built. A bump toward a newer crates.io release would leave the manifest asking for a version the patched revision does not provide, which fails to resolve. The revisions move through .github/workflows/sync-siblings.yml instead, which rewrites the patch table and regenerates Cargo.lock together.
